hook: A news report says the government's deficit fell this year, and in the same breath that the national debt hit a record. Both can be true. A deficit is one year's gap between what a government pays out and what it collects; the debt is the total it owes from every year so far. Shrinking a deficit still adds to the debt, just more slowly.

prereq.q: Which is an example of contractionary fiscal policy?
prereq.why: Higher taxes lower disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

prereq.q: How do automatic stabilizers act in a recession?
options: Tax revenue falls and transfer payments rise with no new law
Tax rates rise automatically to balance the budget
The central bank lowers its policy rate
prereq.why: Progressive taxes collect less and benefits such as unemployment compensation pay out more as incomes fall.

chain.cause: Outlays exceed tax revenue in a year
chain.effect: the government runs a budget deficit
it borrows the difference by selling bonds
the national debt rises by the amount of the deficit

chain.cause: A recession lowers revenue and raises transfers
chain.effect: the deficit widens even with no new law

ideas: Budget balance = tax revenue - outlays. Negative is a deficit, positive a surplus, zero a balanced budget. Outlays include spending, transfer payments and interest on the debt.
The national debt is the total owed: past deficits minus past surpluses. A deficit is a flow over one year; the debt is a stock at a point in time.
A smaller deficit still raises the debt. Only a surplus lowers it.
Expansionary fiscal policy and recessions (through automatic stabilizers) widen deficits; contractionary policy and expansions shrink them.

misconception.wrong: When the deficit falls, the national debt falls.
misconception.right: The debt falls only when the government runs a surplus. A smaller deficit means the debt grows more slowly, because the government is still borrowing.

summary: A budget deficit is one year's excess of government outlays over tax revenue; a surplus is the reverse. The government borrows to cover a deficit, so the national debt, a stock, rises by each deficit and falls only with a surplus. Expansionary fiscal policy and recessions widen deficits, contractionary policy and expansions narrow them, and interest on the debt is itself part of outlays.
